content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a comprehensive guideline to address the assessment and management of infants and children under five years of age who present to primary health-care facilities. This guideline focuses on reducing the risk of overweight and obesity in children, particularly in settings where both undernutrition and overnutrition are prevalent. The recommendations aim to inform health-care providers, policymakers, and program managers on evidence-based practices to improve child health outcomes. The guideline was developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology, which involved systematic reviews of up-to-date evidence. A steering committee and a 17-member expert group were convened to draft and finalize the recommendations. Potential conflicts of interest among group members were disclosed, and one conflict was identified. The member involved was allowed to participate in discussions but was excluded from voting if required. The recommendations emphasize the importance of equity and human rights in health care, particularly for infants and children presenting with clinical problems. The WHO recognizes that while ill health often results from broader social and nutritional contexts, this guideline focuses on addressing clinical issues within a medical framework. Broader solutions to these underlying issues are acknowledged but are beyond the scope of this guideline. Key recommendations include: 1. Anthropometric Assessment: However, mid-upper arm circumference is not recommended for identifying overweight or obesity due to the lack of validated cut-off values. 2. Nutrition Counseling: Caregivers of all children under five should receive general nutrition counseling, including the promotion of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and continued breastfeeding up to 24 months or beyond. Specific counseling for children with stunting is not separately recommended. 3. Supplementary Foods: The provision of supplementary foods for treating stunting or moderate acute malnutrition in primary care settings is not recommended, except in areas with high prevalence of wasting or food insecurity. In such cases, supplementary foods may be part of a broader care plan that includes clinical treatment, nutritional counseling, and follow-up. 4. Management of Overweight and Obesity: Health workers should provide nutrition and physical activity counseling to caregivers of overweight children under five. Obese children should be assessed, and an appropriate management plan should be developed, either at the primary care level (if the health worker is adequately trained) or through referral to specialized facilities. The guideline also highlights the global epidemic of childhood obesity, which affects all regions, including countries where undernutrition remains common. In 2016, an estimated 41 million children under five were overweight or obese, with nearly half living in Asia and a quarter in Africa. The rise in childhood obesity is attributed to unhealthy diets, physical inactivity, urbanization, and other lifestyle changes. Overweight and obesity in childhood are associated with immediate and long-term health risks, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and premature death in adulthood. The WHO emphasizes the importance of addressing both undernutrition and overnutrition in an integrated manner. Interventions should consider the long-term health consequences of childhood malnutrition and avoid inadvertently increasing the risk of obesity and noncommunicable diseases later in life. It is intended for use in lowand middle-resource settings and will inform revisions to existing WHO training materials, such as the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) approach. Successful implementation will require adequate training and capacity development for health-care workers, as well as systematic monitoring and evaluation of programs to identify and address challenges. In summary, this guideline provides evidence-based recommendations to support health workers in assessing and managing the nutritional status of children under five, with a focus on preventing overweight and obesity while addressing undernutrition. It underscores the need for a balanced approach that considers both immediate and long-term health outcomes.
